slides.narration: A diver feels her ears squeezed as she goes deeper. A water tower sends water to the top floor of a building. An aeroplane stays in the air. In this part we learn what pressure is, how it changes with depth, how a small force can lift a car, and how the pressure in moving water is linked to its speed.

slides.heading: Pressure
slides.body_md: Pressure is the normal force on a surface divided by its area: $P = \dfrac{F}{A}$.
bullets: It is a scalar: in a fluid at rest it acts equally in all directions at a point and always at right angles to any surface.
SI unit: pascal (Pa) = newton per square metre.
The same force on a smaller area gives a larger pressure: a needle pierces, a flat palm does not.

visual.alt: Table of pressure units: pascal, atmosphere, bar, millimetre of mercury and metre of water with their values in pascal

slides.narration: Pressure is the force pressing at right angles on a surface, divided by the area of that surface. It is a scalar. In a fluid at rest it pushes equally in every direction at a given point. Its unit is the pascal, one newton per square metre. The same force over a smaller area gives a larger pressure, which is why a needle goes in easily.

slides.heading: Pressure at a depth
slides.body_md: Take a vertical column of liquid of area $A$ and height $h$ at rest. Its weight $\rho A h g$ is carried by the extra pressure on its base:
bullets: $P_0$ is the pressure at the free surface (usually the atmosphere); $\rho g h$ is the **gauge pressure** at depth $h$.
Pressure depends only on depth, density and g: not on the shape of the vessel or the amount of liquid.
All points at the same level in the same liquid, at rest and connected, have the same pressure.

slides.narration: Think of a vertical column of liquid. Its weight must be carried by the pressure difference between its bottom and its top. That gives the pressure at depth h as the surface pressure plus rho g h. The extra part depends only on the depth, the density and g, not on the shape of the vessel. Points at the same level in a connected liquid at rest have the same pressure.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a tap below a tank
slides.body_md: An open overhead tank in a Pune apartment block has its water surface 18 m above a tap on the ground floor. Take $\rho = 1000$ kg m$^{-3}$, $g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$ and $P_0 = 1.013 \times 10^{5}$ Pa. Find the gauge pressure and the absolute pressure at the tap.
bullets: Gauge pressure $= \rho g h = 1000 \times 9.8 \times 18 = 1.764 \times 10^{5}$ Pa.
Absolute pressure $= P_0 + \rho g h = 1.013 \times 10^{5} + 1.764 \times 10^{5} = 2.777 \times 10^{5}$ Pa.
The absolute pressure is about 2.7 times the atmospheric pressure.

visual.alt: Straight line of absolute pressure in water against depth, starting at 101.3 kilopascals at the surface and rising by 9.8 kilopascals for every metre
visual.caption: Each 10 m of water adds about one atmosphere.

slides.narration: The water surface is eighteen metres above the tap. The gauge pressure is rho g h, which is one thousand times nine point eight times eighteen, about one point seven six times ten to the five pascal. Adding the atmospheric pressure of one point zero one three times ten to the five gives about two point seven eight times ten to the five pascal. That is almost three atmospheres.

slides.heading: Atmospheric, gauge and absolute pressure
slides.body_md: A barometer is a closed tube of mercury inverted in a trough: the column stands at the height where its pressure equals the atmosphere.
bullets: Standard atmosphere: $1.013 \times 10^{5}$ Pa $\approx$ 760 mm of mercury.
Absolute pressure = gauge pressure + atmospheric pressure. A tyre gauge or a blood-pressure meter shows gauge pressure.
The height of a barometer column does not change if the tube is tilted or is wider; only the vertical height counts.

slides.narration: A mercury barometer is a closed glass tube, filled with mercury and turned upside down in a trough. The column stands at the height where its weight per unit area equals the atmospheric pressure. Absolute pressure is gauge pressure plus atmospheric pressure. Tilting or widening the tube does not change the vertical height of the column.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: how tall is a barometer column?
slides.body_md: Find the height of the column of mercury ($13\,600$ kg m$^{-3}$) and, for comparison, of water that atmospheric pressure $1.013 \times 10^{5}$ Pa can support. Use $g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$.
bullets: Mercury: $h = \dfrac{P_0}{\rho g} = \dfrac{1.013 \times 10^{5}}{13600 \times 9.8} \approx 0.760$ m, that is 760 mm.
Water: $h = \dfrac{1.013 \times 10^{5}}{1000 \times 9.8} \approx 10.3$ m, about 13.6 times taller.
This is why mercury, a very dense liquid, is used in barometers.

rows: ρ g h = 176400 Pa at 18 m depth
760 mm of mercury, 10.3 m of water

slides.narration: For mercury, divide the atmospheric pressure by rho g: about zero point seven six metres, which is seven hundred and sixty millimetres. A water barometer would need a column of about ten point three metres, thirteen point six times taller, because water is that much less dense. That is why barometers use mercury.

slides.heading: Pascal’s law
slides.body_md: A change of pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to every point of the fluid and to the walls of the container.
bullets: It follows from the fact that pressure in a fluid at rest depends only on depth: add the same extra pressure at the top and every point gains the same amount.
It is the principle behind the hydraulic lift, the hydraulic press and hydraulic brakes.
Liquids are nearly incompressible, so the pressure change is passed on at once.

rows: a small push lifts a heavy load
same pressure, larger area gives larger force
a pedal push acts on every wheel
pressure reaches all slave pistons equally
a small force squeezes metal sheets

visual.alt: Table of applications of Pascal law: hydraulic lift, hydraulic brake and hydraulic press

slides.narration: Pascal’s law says that when you change the pressure on an enclosed fluid, the change reaches every point of the fluid and the walls of the vessel undiminished. It follows from the fact that pressure at rest depends only on depth. Hydraulic lifts, presses and brakes all use it, and they work well because liquids are almost incompressible.

slides.heading: The hydraulic lift
slides.body_md: The same pressure acts on both pistons, so $\dfrac{F_1}{A_1} = \dfrac{F_2}{A_2}$ and $F_2 = F_1\,\dfrac{A_2}{A_1}$.
bullets: A small force on the narrow piston gives a large force on the wide piston: a force multiplier.
The liquid is incompressible, so the volumes moved are equal: $A_1 d_1 = A_2 d_2$. The narrow piston moves farther.
Work in = work out: the lift multiplies force, not energy.

slides.narration: The pressure is the same on both pistons, so the force on the wide piston is the force on the narrow piston times the ratio of the areas. A small push thus supports a heavy load. But the liquid volume is conserved, so the narrow piston must travel much farther than the wide one. The work done on each piston is the same. The machine multiplies force, not energy.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: lifting a car
slides.body_md: A garage lift has a narrow piston of radius 3.0 cm and a wide piston of radius 12 cm. A car of mass 1500 kg stands on the wide piston ($g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$). Find the force on the narrow piston, the distance it moves when the car rises 0.15 m, and the gauge pressure in the liquid.
bullets: $W = mg = 1500 \times 9.8 = 14700$ N; area ratio $= \left(\dfrac{12}{3.0}\right)^2 = 16$.
$d_1 = 16 \times 0.15 = 2.4$ m; work $= 919 \times 2.4 \approx 2205$ J on each side.
$P = \dfrac{F_1}{A_1} = \dfrac{918.75}{\pi (0.030)^2} \approx 3.25 \times 10^{5}$ Pa (gauge).

visual.alt: Table comparing force, distance moved and work for the narrow and the wide piston of a hydraulic lift

slides.narration: The car weighs fourteen thousand seven hundred newtons. The radius ratio is four, so the area ratio is sixteen, and the force needed on the narrow piston is about nine hundred and nineteen newtons. To raise the car by fifteen centimetres, the narrow piston must move sixteen times as far, two point four metres. The work is about two thousand two hundred joules on both sides.

slides.heading: Streamline flow and the equation of continuity
slides.body_md: In **steady (streamline) flow** every particle passing a point follows the same path, the streamline; streamlines never cross.
bullets: For an incompressible fluid the volume flowing per second, A v, is the same at every cross-section.
Where the pipe narrows the streamlines crowd together and the fluid speeds up.
This is the idea behind putting a thumb over the end of a garden hose.

slides.narration: In steady streamline flow each particle follows the same path, and the paths never cross. Where a pipe narrows, the streamlines crowd together and the fluid moves faster, as when you put a thumb over a garden hose.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a fire hose
slides.body_md: Water flows at 2.0 m s$^{-1}$ through a hose of radius 3.0 cm that ends in a nozzle of radius 1.5 cm. Find the speed at the nozzle and the volume flow rate.
bullets: $Q = A_1 v_1 = \pi (0.030)^2 \times 2.0 \approx 5.65 \times 10^{-3}$ m$^3$ s$^{-1}$, about 5.65 litres per second.

visual.alt: Table of the radius, area and water speed in the wide hose and in the narrow nozzle

slides.narration: The radius halves at the nozzle, so the area falls to a quarter and the speed rises to four times, eight metres per second. The volume flow rate is the hose area times the hose speed, about five point six five times ten to the minus three cubic metres per second, which is about five point six five litres every second.

slides.heading: Bernoulli’s principle
slides.body_md: For steady, non-viscous, incompressible flow along a streamline, the energy per unit volume is constant:
bullets: It is the work–energy theorem for a flowing fluid: pressure does work, and the energy goes into speed and height.
At the same height, higher speed means lower pressure.
It does not apply to turbulent or strongly viscous flow, or to compressible flow.

visual.alt: Table of the three terms of the Bernoulli equation, each an energy per unit volume

slides.narration: Bernoulli’s principle is the work energy theorem for a moving fluid. Along a streamline, pressure plus half rho v squared plus rho g h stays constant. It assumes steady flow of a fluid that is incompressible and has no viscosity. At the same height, a faster fluid has a lower pressure. It does not hold for turbulent flow.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: speed of efflux
slides.body_md: An open tank of water is 2.0 m deep. A small hole is made 0.50 m below the surface. Find the speed of the water leaving the hole and where the jet lands on the ground, taking the tank base on the ground ($g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$).
bullets: Bernoulli between the surface ($P_0$, $v \approx 0$) and the hole ($P_0$, $v$): $v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 0.50} \approx 3.13$ m s$^{-1}$ (Torricelli).
The jet leaves horizontally and falls 1.5 m: $t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 1.5}{9.8}} \approx 0.553$ s.
Range $R = v t \approx 3.13 \times 0.553 \approx 1.73$ m.

slides.narration: Apply Bernoulli between the surface and the hole. Both are open to the air, and the surface moves very slowly, so the speed at the hole is the square root of two g h, about three point one three metres per second. That is the speed of a body that fell freely through the same depth. The jet then falls one point five metres, which takes about half a second, and lands about one point seven metres away.

slides.heading: Where should the hole be?
slides.body_md: For a hole at depth $h$ in a tank of depth $H$ standing on the ground: $R = 2\sqrt{h\,(H - h)}$.
bullets: The range is largest, equal to H, when the hole is half-way down (h = H/2).
Holes at depths h and H − h give the same range.
The speed depends only on the depth of the hole, not on the density of the liquid.

x.label: hole depth h below the surface (m)

visual.alt: Range of the jet against the depth of the hole in a tank 2.0 metres deep: a symmetric arch with its maximum of 2.0 metres at a depth of 1.0 metre
visual.caption: Holes at h and H − h give the same range.

slides.narration: The range of the jet depends on the speed and on the time of fall. A hole near the surface gives a slow jet that falls a long way; a hole near the base gives a fast jet that falls only a little. The range is largest when the hole is half way down. Two holes at equal distances above and below the middle give the same range.

slides.heading: The Venturi meter
slides.body_md: A horizontal pipe with a narrow throat. Continuity makes the fluid faster in the throat; Bernoulli makes the pressure lower there.
bullets: The height difference Δh of the liquid in two open tubes measures the pressure difference.
With $v_2 = v_1 A_1/A_2$ one gets $v_1 = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(P_1 - P_2)}{\rho\,[(A_1/A_2)^2 - 1]}}$, and the flow rate $Q = A_1 v_1$.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: reading a Venturi meter
slides.body_md: Water flows through a horizontal pipe of diameter 8.0 cm with a throat of diameter 4.0 cm. The pressure in the throat is 7500 Pa lower than in the wide part. Find the speeds and the flow rate ($\rho = 1000$ kg m$^{-3}$).

visual.alt: Table of diameters, speeds and the pressure difference of a Venturi meter

slides.narration: The diameter ratio is two, so the area ratio is four and the throat speed is four times the speed in the wide part. Half rho times sixteen minus one times v one squared equals the pressure difference. That gives a speed of one metre per second in the wide part and four metres per second in the throat. The flow rate is about five litres per second.

slides.heading: Dynamic lift
slides.body_md: An aerofoil, a spinning ball or a tilted kite pushes the air so that the speed is higher on one side.
bullets: Streamlines crowd above the wing: the air is faster and the pressure lower there; below the wing the pressure is higher.
Lift $\approx (P_{\text{below}} - P_{\text{above}})\,A = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho\,(v_{\text{above}}^2 - v_{\text{below}}^2)\,A$.
A spinning ball drags air round with it and curves in flight (the Magnus effect).

slides.heading: Summary — Part 1
slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: P = F/A; at depth h: P = P₀ + ρ g h
gauge = P − P₀; P₀ = ρ g h = 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa = 760 mm Hg
pressure change is transmitted undiminished; F₂ = F₁ A₂/A₁
A₁v₁ = A₂v₂: narrower pipe, faster flow
P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant along a streamline
efflux v = √(2gh); Venturi meter; dynamic lift

visual.alt: Summary table of pressure, Pascal law, continuity and Bernoulli principle

slides.narration: To sum up. Pressure is force per unit area, and at depth h in a liquid it is the surface pressure plus rho g h. Pascal’s law lets a hydraulic device multiply force, though never energy. For steady flow the product of area and speed is constant, and Bernoulli’s principle keeps the sum of pressure, kinetic energy and potential energy per unit volume constant along a streamline.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 1
bullets: State whether you are finding gauge or absolute pressure, and add P₀ only for absolute.
In hydraulic problems use the area ratio (radius squared), and remember the distances move in the inverse ratio.
Check the conditions before using Bernoulli: steady flow, no viscosity, along one streamline.
Convert cm to m and L to m³ before substituting.

slides.narration: Always say whether the pressure is gauge or absolute. In hydraulic problems the force ratio is the ratio of the areas, which is the square of the ratio of the radii, and the distances go the other way. Check that the flow is steady and the fluid is non viscous before using Bernoulli. And change centimetres to metres and litres to cubic metres first.

slides.narration: Honey pours slowly, water pours fast. A raindrop falls at a steady speed. A needle can float on water, and water climbs up the thin wick of a lamp. In this part we meet viscosity, which opposes the flow of a fluid, and surface tension, which makes a liquid surface behave like a stretched skin.

slides.heading: Viscosity
slides.body_md: Viscosity is the internal friction of a fluid: layers moving at different speeds drag on each other.
bullets: $F$ is the force on a plate of area $A$ moving at speed $v$ over a fluid layer of thickness $d$; $v/d$ is the velocity gradient.
$\eta$ is the coefficient of viscosity; SI unit pascal second (Pa s) = N s m$^{-2}$.
The layer next to a solid surface moves with it; layers farther away are dragged along.

slides.narration: Imagine a fluid between a fixed plate and a moving plate. The layer touching each plate moves with it, and the layers in between slide over each other, with speed growing steadily from zero to the plate speed. The force needed to keep the top plate moving is eta times the area times the velocity gradient. The coefficient eta is the viscosity.

slides.heading: Viscosity of liquids and gases
slides.body_md: Typical values of η at about 20 °C:
bullets: Liquids become less viscous as the temperature rises (honey flows faster when warm).
Gases become more viscous as the temperature rises, because faster molecules exchange more momentum between layers.
Viscosity is the reason a flowing fluid needs a pressure difference to keep moving.

rows: η of a gas rises as it gets hotter
η of a liquid falls as it gets hotter
about 1400 times as viscous as water

visual.alt: Table of the coefficient of viscosity of air, water and glycerine at about twenty degrees Celsius and how it changes with temperature

slides.narration: Water has a viscosity of about one thousandth of a pascal second. Glycerine is more than a thousand times as viscous. Air is far less viscous than water. When the temperature rises, the viscosity of a liquid falls, but the viscosity of a gas rises. Viscosity is why a pressure difference is needed to keep a fluid flowing through a pipe.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: sliding a plate on oil
slides.body_md: A flat plate of area 0.040 m$^2$ is pulled at 0.50 m s$^{-1}$ over a layer of oil 2.0 mm thick on a fixed plate. The viscosity of the oil is 0.80 Pa s. Find the force needed.
bullets: Velocity gradient $= \dfrac{v}{d} = \dfrac{0.50}{0.002} = 250$ s$^{-1}$.
$F = \eta A \dfrac{v}{d} = 0.80 \times 0.040 \times 250 = 8.0$ N.
Halving the oil thickness doubles the force needed.

slides.heading: Stokes’ law and terminal velocity
slides.body_md: A small sphere of radius $r$ moving at speed $v$ through a fluid feels the viscous drag $F = 6\pi\eta r v$ (Stokes’ law).
bullets: A falling sphere speeds up until weight = upthrust + drag; then the net force is zero and it falls at the constant **terminal velocity** $v_t$.
$\rho$ is the density of the sphere and $\sigma$ that of the fluid.
Stokes’ law holds for small spheres at low speed, where the flow is smooth.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a steel ball in oil
slides.body_md: A steel ball of radius 1.0 mm (density 7800 kg m$^{-3}$) is released in oil of density 900 kg m$^{-3}$ and viscosity 0.40 Pa s. Find its terminal velocity ($g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$) and check that the flow is smooth.
bullets: $v_t = \dfrac{2 r^2 (\rho - \sigma) g}{9\eta} = \dfrac{2 \times (1.0 \times 10^{-3})^2 \times 6900 \times 9.8}{9 \times 0.40} \approx 0.0376$ m s$^{-1}$, that is 3.76 cm s$^{-1}$.
Reynolds number $\approx \dfrac{\sigma v_t (2r)}{\eta} = \dfrac{900 \times 0.0376 \times 0.0020}{0.40} \approx 0.17$, far below 1: Stokes’ law is valid.
It reaches this speed within about $\tau = \dfrac{2\rho r^2}{9\eta} \approx 4.33$ ms.

visual.alt: Speed of a steel ball released from rest in oil: it rises quickly and levels off at the terminal speed of 3.76 centimetres per second within about twenty milliseconds
visual.caption: The speed approaches v_t and never exceeds it.

slides.narration: Put the numbers into the terminal velocity formula: radius one millimetre, density difference six thousand nine hundred, viscosity zero point four. The result is about three point seven six centimetres per second. The Reynolds number is only about zero point one seven, so the flow is smooth and Stokes’ law applies. The ball reaches this speed in a few milliseconds.

slides.heading: What controls the terminal velocity?
slides.body_md: From $v_t = \dfrac{2r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{9\eta}$:
bullets: Bigger spheres fall faster: v_t grows as r², so a drop of twice the radius falls four times as fast.
A more viscous fluid slows the sphere: v_t varies as 1/η.
If the sphere is lighter than the fluid, ρ − σ is negative and it rises with a terminal speed (a bubble in honey).
A raindrop in air also reaches a terminal speed, which is why rain does not hurt.

rows: v_t = 0: the ball does not sink

visual.alt: Table showing how the terminal speed depends on radius, viscosity and density difference

slides.narration: The terminal speed grows with the square of the radius, so a drop of twice the radius falls four times as fast. It falls with the inverse of the viscosity, so honey slows a ball much more than water does. If the sphere is lighter than the fluid, the speed turns negative and the sphere rises, as a bubble does in honey. Rain reaches a terminal speed in air too.

slides.heading: Streamline and turbulent flow: the Reynolds number
slides.body_md: Flow in a pipe is smooth (**laminar**) at low speed and becomes irregular (**turbulent**) at high speed. The Reynolds number decides:
bullets: Re below about 1000: laminar. Above about 2000: turbulent. In between: unstable.
The speed at which the flow turns turbulent is the **critical velocity**.
Turbulence increases the resistance to flow; Bernoulli’s equation does not apply to it.

rows: water, d = 1.0 cm, v = 0.05 m s⁻¹
water, d = 1.5 cm, v = 1.5 m s⁻¹

visual.alt: Table of two Reynolds numbers for water in pipes and the kind of flow each gives

slides.narration: At low speed a fluid flows in smooth layers. At high speed the flow becomes irregular and swirling. The Reynolds number, density times speed times pipe diameter over viscosity, decides which. Below about one thousand the flow is laminar, and above about two thousand it is turbulent. The speed at which turbulence begins is called the critical velocity.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: laminar or turbulent?
slides.body_md: Water ($\rho = 1000$ kg m$^{-3}$, $\eta = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}$ Pa s) flows through a pipe of diameter 1.0 cm at 0.050 m s$^{-1}$, and through a tap pipe of diameter 1.5 cm at 1.5 m s$^{-1}$. Classify each flow.
bullets: $Re_1 = \dfrac{1000 \times 0.050 \times 0.01}{1.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 500$: below 1000, so laminar.
$Re_2 = \dfrac{1000 \times 1.5 \times 0.015}{1.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 22500$: far above 2000, so turbulent.
A slowly trickling tap is laminar; a fully open tap is turbulent.

For the tap pipe at one point five metres per second the number is twenty two thousand five hundred, far above two thousand, so the flow is turbulent. A trickle is laminar; a fully open tap is turbulent.

slides.heading: Surface tension
slides.body_md: Molecules inside a liquid are pulled equally in all directions; those at the surface are pulled inward, so the surface acts like a stretched elastic skin.
bullets: Surface tension S is the force per unit length acting along a line drawn on the surface, at right angles to the line and tangent to the surface: SI unit N m⁻¹.
A film with two surfaces (a soap film) pulls on a wire of length l with force F = 2 S l.
It makes small drops spherical and lets a needle float on water.

slides.heading: Surface energy and surface tension of liquids
slides.body_md: Surface energy per unit area equals the surface tension: $S = \dfrac{W}{\Delta A}$ (J m$^{-2}$ = N m$^{-1}$).
bullets: Making a new surface needs work against the inward pull, so a liquid takes the shape of least surface area: a sphere for a free drop.
Surface tension falls as the temperature rises and when a detergent is added.
When small drops merge into one big drop the total surface area falls, and energy is released.

visual.alt: Table of the surface tension of water, soap solution, ethyl alcohol and mercury

slides.narration: The work needed to create new surface, divided by the area created, is the surface energy per unit area, and it equals the surface tension. A liquid therefore tends to take the shape of the least surface area, a sphere for a free drop. Surface tension falls when the liquid is heated or when detergent is added. Merging drops release energy.

slides.heading: Angle of contact
slides.body_md: Where a liquid surface meets a solid, the **angle of contact** θ is the angle between the solid surface and the tangent to the liquid surface, measured inside the liquid.
bullets: θ < 90°: the liquid wets the solid and spreads (water on clean glass, θ close to 0°).
θ > 90°: the liquid does not wet the solid and bunches up (mercury on glass, about 140°).
The angle depends on the liquid, the solid and the surrounding medium; it is why water beads on a waxed surface.

slides.heading: Excess pressure in a drop and a bubble

bullets: A liquid drop, or an air bubble inside a liquid, has one surface: 2S/R.
A soap bubble has two surfaces (inside and outside the film): 4S/R.
Smaller drops and bubbles have a larger excess pressure.

The excess pressure acting on the flat circle must equal the surface tension pulling along the rim, so the excess pressure is two S over R. A soap bubble has two surfaces, so the pull is doubled and the excess pressure is four S over R. The smaller the bubble, the larger the excess pressure.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a soap bubble and a water drop
slides.body_md: Find the excess pressure inside (a) a soap bubble of radius 1.5 cm in a soap solution with $S = 0.030$ N m$^{-1}$, (b) a water drop of radius 0.50 mm ($S = 0.072$ N m$^{-1}$).
bullets: (a) $\Delta P = \dfrac{4S}{R} = \dfrac{4 \times 0.030}{0.015} = 8$ Pa.
(b) $\Delta P = \dfrac{2S}{R} = \dfrac{2 \times 0.072}{0.0005} = 288$ Pa.
The tiny drop has the greater excess pressure although its surface tension is larger only by a factor of 2.4.

slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: F = η A v/d; unit Pa s; liquids thin out when warm, gases thicken
drag = 6π η r v; v_t = 2r²(ρ − σ)g / 9η
Re = ρ v d / η; laminar below about 1000, turbulent above about 2000

slides.narration: To sum up. Viscous force is eta A v over d. Stokes drag is six pi eta r v, and a falling sphere reaches a terminal speed proportional to the square of its radius. The Reynolds number tells laminar from turbulent flow. Surface tension is force per unit length or energy per unit area, giving excess pressures of two S over R for a drop and four S over R for a soap bubble, and capillary rise two S cos theta over rho g r.

sections.heading: 1. Pressure, pressure at a depth, and Pascal’s law
sections.body_md:
- **Pressure** $P = F/A$ is the normal force per unit area (scalar, unit pascal). In a fluid at rest it acts equally in all directions at a point.
- **Pressure at a depth** $h$ below a free surface: $P = P_0 + \rho g h$. The part $\rho g h$ is the **gauge pressure**; $P$ is the **absolute pressure**. It does not depend on the shape of the vessel, and points at the same level in a connected liquid at rest have the same pressure. For a tap 18 m below an open tank: gauge 1.764 \times 10^{5} Pa, absolute 2.777 \times 10^{5} Pa.
- **Atmospheric pressure** $P_0 = 1.013 \times 10^{5}$ Pa $\approx 760$ mm of mercury. A barometer column has $h = P_0/\rho g$: 0.760 m for mercury (13600 kg m$^{-3}$), 10.3 m for water.
- **Pascal’s law:** a pressure change applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to every point of the fluid and to the container walls.
- **Hydraulic lift:** $F_2 = F_1 A_2/A_1$ and $A_1 d_1 = A_2 d_2$: a force multiplier, but work in equals work out. With radii 3.0 cm and 12 cm a force of 919 N supports 14700 N, and the narrow piston moves 2.4 m for every 0.15 m the load rises. **Hydraulic brakes** send one pedal push to every wheel through the same pressure.

sections.heading: 2. Streamline flow, continuity and Bernoulli’s principle
sections.body_md:
- In **streamline (steady) flow** each particle follows the same path (a streamline); streamlines do not cross. For an incompressible fluid the **equation of continuity** holds: $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$. In a hose of radius 3.0 cm ending in a 1.5 cm nozzle, 2.0 m s$^{-1}$ becomes 8.0 m s$^{-1}$; the flow rate is 5.65 \times 10^{-3} m$^3$ s$^{-1}$.
- **Bernoulli’s principle:** along a streamline of steady, non-viscous, incompressible flow, $P + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g h$ is constant. At the same height, faster flow means lower pressure. It does not hold for turbulent or viscous flow.
- **Speed of efflux (Torricelli):** $v = \sqrt{2gh}$ for a hole at depth $h$ below an open surface (3.13 m s$^{-1}$ at 0.50 m). The range on the ground is $R = 2\sqrt{h(H-h)}$, largest for $h = H/2$; here 1.73 m.
- **Venturi meter:** the pressure drop in the throat gives the speed, $v_1 = \sqrt{2\Delta P/[\rho((A_1/A_2)^2 - 1)]}$; for areas in the ratio 4 and $\Delta P = 7500$ Pa the speeds are 1.0 and 4.0 m s$^{-1}$.
- **Dynamic lift:** faster air over the upper surface of an aerofoil gives lower pressure there, so the net force is upward; a spinning ball curves because of a similar pressure difference (Magnus effect).

sections.heading: 3. Viscosity, Stokes’ law and terminal velocity
sections.body_md:
- **Viscosity** is the internal friction of a fluid. For a plate of area $A$ moving at speed $v$ over a layer of thickness $d$: $F = \eta A v/d$; $\eta$ has unit Pa s. Example: 0.040 m$^2$, 0.50 m s$^{-1}$, 2.0 mm of oil with $\eta = 0.80$ Pa s needs 8.0 N. Liquids become less viscous when heated; gases more viscous.
- **Stokes’ law:** the drag on a small sphere is $F = 6\pi\eta r v$.
- **Terminal velocity:** a falling sphere reaches the constant speed at which weight = upthrust + drag, $v_t = 2r^2(\rho - \sigma)g/9\eta$. A steel ball of radius 1.0 mm in oil ($\sigma = 900$ kg m$^{-3}$, $\eta = 0.40$ Pa s) has $v_t \approx 3.76$ cm s$^{-1}$. It varies as $r^2$ and as $1/\eta$.
- **Reynolds number** $Re = \rho v d/\eta$ decides the type of flow in a pipe: laminar below about 1000, turbulent above about 2000. Water in a 1.0 cm pipe at 0.05 m s$^{-1}$ has $Re = 500$ (laminar); in a 1.5 cm pipe at 1.5 m s$^{-1}$, $Re = 22500$ (turbulent). The speed at which turbulence begins is the critical velocity.

key_terms.definition_md: The constant η in F = η A v/d; unit pascal second.
The constant speed reached when the net force on a falling body is zero.
ρ v d / η: the ratio that decides whether flow is laminar or turbulent.

sections.heading: 4. Surface tension, surface energy, angle of contact and capillarity
sections.body_md:
- **Surface tension** $S = F/l$: the force per unit length on a line drawn on the surface (N m$^{-1}$); it is also the **surface energy** per unit area, $S = W/\Delta A$. A soap film with two surfaces pulls on a wire of length $l$ with $F = 2Sl$: for $l = 8.0$ cm and $S = 0.030$ N m$^{-1}$, 4.80 \times 10^{-3} N; pulling it 5.0 cm does 2.40 \times 10^{-4} J of work.
- **Angle of contact** $\theta$: between the solid surface and the tangent to the liquid surface, measured inside the liquid. $\theta < 90^\circ$: the liquid wets the solid; $\theta > 90^\circ$: it does not (mercury on glass, about 140$^\circ$).
- **Excess pressure:** drop or air bubble in a liquid $2S/R$; soap bubble (two surfaces) $4S/R$. A soap bubble of radius 1.5 cm with $S = 0.030$ N m$^{-1}$: 8 Pa.
- **Capillary rise:** $h = 2S\cos\theta/(\rho g r)$. Water ($\theta \approx 0^\circ$) in a tube of radius 0.50 mm rises 2.94 cm; mercury ($\theta = 140^\circ$) in a 1.0 mm tube is depressed by 5.35 mm. The rise varies as $1/r$.
- Surface tension decreases as the temperature rises and when detergent is added; merging drops lose surface area and release energy.

key_terms.definition_md: Force per unit length along a line on a liquid surface, or surface energy per unit area.
The angle between the solid surface and the tangent to the liquid surface, measured inside the liquid.
The rise (or fall) of a liquid in a narrow tube because of surface tension.
